chief_complaint: chronic sinusitis with bloody nasal crusting, cough with blood, and kidney failure
hpi_details: 52M presenting with several weeks of chronic sinus crusting and bloody discharge progressing to saddle nose deformity, with new hemoptysis and hematuria with facial and leg edema.
ideas: He thinks he has a severe, neglected sinus infection that has spread down into his chest and lungs.
concerns: He is worried that coughing up blood means he has an aggressive lung cancer that will prevent him from providing for his family.
expectations: He hopes to get a chest scan and a prescription for strong antibiotics to clear up the bleeding and swelling right away.

clinical_knowledge.topic: Granulomatosis with Polyangiitis (GPA) evaluation and management
core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Granulomatosis with Polyangiitis (GPA) is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.

Standard management emphasizes immediate hospital admission and urgent induction immunosuppression for pulmonary-renal syndrome without delaying treatment for biopsy confirmation, adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: chronic sinusitis with bloody nasal crusting, cough with blood, and kidney failure
Key HPI features: 52M presenting with several weeks of chronic sinus crusting and bloody discharge progressing to saddle nose deformity, with new hemoptysis and hematuria with facial and leg edema.

Objective/Exam findings: Vitals assessed for hypertension, tachypnea, and hypoxia. Saddle nose deformity with nasal septal perforation and crusted nasal mucosa. Lung exam with crackles, possible signs of alveolar hemorrhage. Peripheral edema. Urinalysis shows hematuria, RBC casts, and proteinuria. Skin exam for palpable purpura. No focal neurologic deficits.
Relevant background/PMH: No significant chronic medical history
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Granulomatosis with Polyangiitis (GPA).
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Microscopic polyangiitis without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Hemoptysis with kidney involvement — signals life-threatening pulmonary-renal syndrome.
management_principles: Pulmonary-renal syndrome (hemoptysis plus hematuria/RBC casts) is a medical emergency requiring same-day hospital admission and urgent multidisciplinary evaluation
Obtain ANCA serology, renal function, urinalysis with microscopy, and chest imaging urgently; pursue tissue biopsy for confirmation when feasible without delaying life-saving treatment

Initiate induction immunosuppression (high-dose glucocorticoids plus rituximab or cyclophosphamide) under specialist direction; do not delay treatment awaiting biopsy in life-threatening presentations
Consider plasma exchange for severe alveolar hemorrhage or rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis, and monitor closely for respiratory failure or the need for dialysis.
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

reference_soap.subjective: 52M presenting with several weeks of chronic sinus crusting and bloody discharge progressing to saddle nose deformity, with new hemoptysis and hematuria with facial and leg edema.
reference_soap.objective: Vitals assessed for hypertension, tachypnea, and hypoxia. Saddle nose deformity with nasal septal perforation and crusted nasal mucosa. Lung exam with crackles, possible signs of alveolar hemorrhage. Peripheral edema. Urinalysis shows hematuria, RBC casts, and proteinuria. Skin exam for palpable purpura.
reference_soap.assessment: Clinical presentation (sinus/nasal involvement, hemoptysis, hematuria with RBC casts) highly concerning for ANCA-associated vasculitis (granulomatosis with polyangiitis) with pulmonary-renal syndrome, a medical emergency; confirmatory ANCA serology and biopsy pending.
reference_soap.plan: Admit immediately given the pulmonary-renal syndrome. Obtain urgent ANCA serology, renal function, urinalysis with microscopy, and chest imaging, and pursue biopsy for confirmation when feasible. Initiate induction immunosuppression (high-dose glucocorticoids plus rituximab or cyclophosphamide) under specialist direction without delay, consider plasma exchange for severe alveolar hemorrhage or rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis, and arrange nephrology/rheumatology co-management with monitoring for respiratory failure or need for dialysis.

learning_objectives: Recognize clinical features and diagnostic criteria of Granulomatosis with Polyangiitis GPA Wegener
Formulate prioritized differential diagnosis for chronic sinusitis with bloody nasal crusting, cough with blood, and kidney failure
Select appropriate urgent laboratory (ANCA serology, renal function, urinalysis) and imaging studies for suspected pulmonary-renal vasculitis
Implement evidence-based acute and long-term management strategies

teaching.one_liner: An ANCA-associated small-vessel vasculitis classically affecting the sinuses, lungs, and kidneys — sinus crusting and saddle-nose deformity, hemoptysis, and hematuria with red cell casts together should trigger urgent testing for c-ANCA/PR3.
red_flags: Hemoptysis with kidney involvement — signals life-threatening pulmonary-renal syndrome

must_ask.say: Have you had chronic sinus problems with bloody crusting?
Have you coughed up any blood?
Have you noticed blood in your urine, or foaminess?
How long has this been developing?
Any fever, weight loss, or joint pain?

history.answer: I've been coughing up blood for the past few days, and my nose has been plugged with bloody crusts for weeks.
The blood comes straight up when I cough from my chest; I am definitely not vomiting it or spitting blood from my mouth.
I bring up about one or two tablespoons of blood every time I have a coughing fit, roughly four or five times a day.
It looks bright red and is mixed with pink frothy phlegm; there are no food bits in it.
The blood in my cough started four days ago and has been happening every single day since then.
I have had a mild dry cough for about a month, but over the last week it became much heavier and started bringing up phlegm.
No, I haven't had large amounts of foul-smelling or thick yellow pus.
I haven't had severe shaking chills, but I've felt warm, feverish, and generally unwell.
I've unintentionally lost about four kilograms over the past two months, and I wake up drenched in sweat and constantly tired.
I don't have sharp stabbing chest pain, but I feel winded and tight in my chest even just walking to the bathroom.
history.topic: Shortness of breath and chest pain

history.answer: No, neither of my legs hurts or looks swollen compared to the other, and I haven't had recent surgery or long flights.
I have to sleep propped up on two pillows now because lying flat makes me feel like I can't catch my breath.
My nose has felt blocked and painful for several weeks with dark bloody crusts, and lately the bridge of my nose looks like it collapsed inward.
Over the past few days my urine has turned dark brownish like cola, I'm peeing less, and my face and ankles have gotten puffy.
No bleeding from my gums, no nosebleeds out the front, and no unusual bruises on my body.
No nausea, heartburn, vomiting, or black tarry stools.
I have never smoked cigarettes or used any tobacco products in my life.
I have never had tuberculosis, and I haven't knowingly been around anyone with chronic cough or TB.
I was born and raised here, haven't traveled overseas recently, and work in a regular clean indoor office.
The sinus congestion and crusting started about two months ago, but the bloody cough, dark urine, and shortness of breath came on rapidly this past week.
I thought maybe I picked up some nasty sinus infection or mold that has spread down into my lungs and chest.
I'm really scared that coughing up blood means I have lung cancer and won't be around to provide for my family.
I'm hoping to get a chest scan today and some strong antibiotics to knock out whatever infection is causing this bleeding.
I have always been healthy and have never had high blood pressure, asthma, kidney trouble, or diabetes.
I have never had any surgeries and have never been hospitalized before.
I do not take any prescription medications, over-the-counter painkillers, aspirin, or supplements.
I have no known allergies to medications, foods, or latex.
I drink one or two glasses of beer socially on weekends, nothing heavy.
I work full-time as an office administrator and live in an apartment with my wife.
There is no history of kidney failure, lung diseases, or autoimmune disorders in my family.

exam.finding: Blood pressure 150/94 mmHg, heart rate 88 beats/min, respiratory rate 22 breaths/min, oxygen saturation 93% on room air, temperature 37.5°C.
Saddle nose deformity of the nasal bridge with mucosal crusting and a nasal septal perforation; posterior pharynx clear without active bleeding.
Mild tenderness over both maxillary sinuses on gentle percussion; frontal sinuses non-tender.
No cervical or supraclavicular lymphadenopathy palpated.
Resonant to percussion across all lung fields bilaterally.
Bilateral fine end-inspiratory crackles heard over the mid and lower lung bases; no wheezing.
Normal S1 and S2 with regular rhythm; no murmurs, rubs, or gallops.
Jugular venous pulse is normal and not elevated.
Bilateral 2+ pitting edema present over both lower legs up to the mid-shins.
Calves are soft, symmetric, and non-tender with no local warmth or swelling.
Scattered palpable purpuric papules noted on both lower legs; no ulcerations.
